summary.text: 对 is the simplified form of 對. The older graph has a disputed interpretation as a hand, a possible tool, and earth, but its earliest meaning is unresolved. Early Western Zhou inscriptions use 對 in formulas with disputed force; later texts use it for “reply” or “answer.” Modern meanings include “correct,” “right,” “facing,” and “opposed.”

formation.text: Traditional 對 has competing analyses. One reads 又 as a hand, 丵 as a possible tool, and 土 as earth in a land-working scene. Another proposes that 丵 and 土 together serve as a sound element, but supplies no reading for 丵 to compare with 對. Neither analysis settles the graph’s earliest meaning.

components.text: In the proposed land-working interpretation of traditional 對, 又 depicts the hand. The modern 又 + 寸 analysis of 对 does not show that the older graph began as a pair of hands.

One analysis identifies 丵 as a digging tool; others identify a punitive instrument or toothed weapon. The object and its original name are uncertain. Another proposal treats 丵 with 土 as a sound element, but provides no reading for 丵 to test against 對.

sound_limitation.text: No reading for 丵 is supplied for comparison with 對, and the alleged implement’s name and pronunciation are unavailable. This limitation does not establish the proposed phonetic role.

components.text: In the proposed land-working scene for traditional 對, 土 depicts earth. Historical forms also show disagreement between 土 and 士, but no specific alteration event or secure sequence among these forms is established.
The received analysis of 𡭊 includes 口 but does not specify its function.
The received analysis of 𡭊 includes 寸. Historical commentary interprets it as measure or rule, but that interpretation does not independently confirm the graph’s earlier structure.

The received account says an alternative form of 對 replaced 口 with 士. Other evidence reports 土 in ancient and clerical forms and questions that account; no specific alteration event or secure sequence is established.

history.text: A modern redraw in oracle-script style shows branching upper strokes, hand-like strokes at lower left, and a long descending stroke on the right. It illustrates the proposed 丵, 又, and 土 analysis but does not establish that interpretation or a sequence of forms.

The received Shuowen account gives 𡭊 as the head form, analyzed as 丵, 口, and 寸, and records 對 as an alternative said to substitute 士 for 口. Other evidence reports 土 in ancient and clerical forms. No specific alteration event or secure ancestor-descendant sequence is established.
In the modern standard, 对 corresponds to traditional 對. The earlier history and adoption pathway of 对 are unresolved.

uncertainties.text: The earliest meaning of 對 is unresolved. Oracle-bone uses have been proposed as a sacrificial or place name, but no specific specimen, context, or meaning is established; land working is not a secure earliest sense.

The land-working interpretation competes with other identifications of 丵 and with a proposal that 丵 and 土 together serve as a phonetic element. No reading for 丵 is supplied to test that proposal against 對’s word reading.

Reuse of the whole graph for “reply” on the basis of sound is not verified: the alleged object’s name and pronunciation are unavailable. Reconstructions of 對 concern the word “respond,” not the alleged implement.

senses.text: Oracle-bone uses have been proposed as a sacrificial or place name, but no specific specimen, context, or meaning is established. The proposed land-working interpretation is not a secure earliest sense.

senses.gloss: meaning in early bronze formulas disputed

senses.text: An inscription uses 對 in a formula following royal rewards. Interpretations include response, acknowledgment or repayment, praise, and ritual action; its precise force remains disputed.

senses.period: Early Western Zhou bronze formulas attest 對; later literary citations are transmitted texts
senses.text: Early Western Zhou bronze inscriptions use 對 in response or acknowledgment formulas, though their precise force is disputed. Later transmitted texts use the word to mean “reply” or “answer”; they do not directly date the surviving graph to the narrative settings they describe.
Modern usage includes “correct” and “right.” When or how these meanings developed is not established.
Modern usage includes “facing” and “opposed.” When or how these meanings developed is not established.

limitations.text: No continuous development is established from proposed land working or boundary marking to bronze formulas or the later reply sense. The precise meaning of the early formulas is disputed.

Reuse of the whole graph for “reply” is not demonstrated. The alleged object’s name and sound are unavailable, and a proposed word-level relation between 對 “respond” and 答 “answer” does not prove graphic borrowing.
The listed modern meanings do not establish a dated chain of semantic development.

overview.text: 对 is the simplified form of 對. Today it means “correct” or “right,” and also “facing” or “opposed.” One disputed analysis pictures a hand, a possible tool, and earth. Sound-based reuse for “reply” is unverified because the old object’s name and pronunciation are unavailable.
